courses.title: Introduction to Biology
courses.description: Explore the fundamentals of life science

content.basic: Biology is the study of living things. It includes cells (the smallest unit of life), organisms, and ecosystems. Everything alive on Earth relies on biological processes.
content.intermediate: Biology examines life at multiple levels: molecular (DNA, proteins), cellular (organelles, metabolism), organismal (anatomy, physiology), and ecological (populations, ecosystems). Evolution explains biodiversity.
content.advanced: Modern biology integrates molecular genetics, systems biology, and evolutionary theory. Key concepts include gene expression, homeostasis, photosynthesis, cellular respiration, and natural selection as mechanisms of adaptation.

content.basic: Math is a language for describing quantities, patterns, and relationships. Basic operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Geometry deals with shapes and space.
content.intermediate: Algebra uses symbols to generalize patterns. Equations allow solving for unknowns. Functions describe relationships between variables. Trigonometry relates angles to side lengths in triangles.
content.advanced: Advanced mathematics includes calculus (studying change), linear algebra (vectors and matrices), differential equations, and complex analysis. These form the basis for physics and engineering.

content.basic: Computers use binary (1s and 0s) to process information. They have hardware (physical parts) and software (programs). The Internet connects computers worldwide allowing data sharing.
content.intermediate: Computers operate through logic gates and algorithms. Programming languages allow humans to give instructions. Operating systems manage resources. Networks enable communication between devices.
content.advanced: Computer science involves algorithm complexity analysis, data structures, artificial intelligence, cryptography, and system architecture. Understanding computation theory explains what problems are solvable computationally.

content.basic: Global citizenship means understanding that we live in an interconnected world. Cultures, economies, and environments are connected. Working together solves global problems.
content.intermediate: Global issues include poverty, climate change, disease, and inequality. International organizations promote cooperation. Sustainable development balances economic growth with environmental protection.
content.advanced: Advanced topics include geopolitics, international law, economic systems, cultural diplomacy, and mechanisms for global governance. Understanding power structures, institutions, and actors enables informed participation in global affairs.

content.basic: Environmental science studies ecosystems, biodiversity, and human impact. Climate is the pattern of weather. Pollution harms air, water, and soil. Conservation protects nature.
content.intermediate: Ecosystems have energy flows and nutrient cycles. Climate change results from greenhouse gas emissions. Renewable energy offers alternatives to fossil fuels. Biodiversity provides ecosystem services.
content.advanced: Advanced study includes biogeochemical cycles, trophic cascades, tipping points in climate systems, ecosystem resilience, and restoration ecology. Understanding anthropogenic impacts guides evidence-based environmental policy.

content.basic: Critical thinking means questioning information and evaluating evidence. Research involves finding reliable sources. Being skeptical helps you avoid false information.
content.intermediate: Analyze sources for bias and credibility. Use logic to evaluate arguments. Distinguish correlation from causation. Scientific method guides research through observation, hypothesis, and testing.
content.advanced: Master research methodologies, statistical analysis, and academic writing. Understand epistemology (how we know things). Evaluate complex claims using multiple perspectives. Practice peer review principles.
